title: Surrounded Regions
directAnswer: Don't hunt for surrounded regions directly — find the ones that are NOT surrounded. Flood-fill from every 'O' on the border (DFS or BFS), marking those border-connected 'O's as safe (e.g. '#'). After the sweep, any 'O' still left is fully enclosed → flip it to 'X'; restore every '#' back to 'O'. One pass to mark, one pass to flip → O(m × n) time. Union-Find with a virtual 'border' node is the alternative.

remember.pattern: Invert the problem: flood-fill the safe (border-connected) region, flip the rest
rules: Solve the **complement**: an 'O' survives only if it can reach the border, so mark border-reachable 'O's first.
Use a **temporary marker** ('#') for safe cells so the final pass can distinguish 'escaped' from 'enclosed'.
Seed the flood fill from **all four edges** — top/bottom rows and left/right columns.
Final pass does two flips: leftover `'O' → 'X'` (captured) and `'#' → 'O'` (restore). Don't forget the restore.
This mutates the board in place and returns **void** — read the signature before coding.
whenToUse: Capture / enclose problems where 'touching the border' means safe
Grid flood fill where the answer is the cells you CAN'T reach from an edge
Region-flipping on a matrix of two states
Any 'connected to the outside' vs 'trapped inside' classification
antiSignals: You need the COUNT of regions, not a flip → plain connected-components (Number of Islands)
Edges/connections arrive incrementally → Union-Find is the natural fit
Movement has weights or you need shortest distance → BFS/Dijkstra, not a simple fill
remember.takeaway: Surrounded Regions teaches the single most useful grid trick after Number of Islands: when 'enclosed' is hard to test directly, flip the question and flood-fill from the border instead. The same border-seeding idea powers Pacific Atlantic Water Flow and Number of Closed Islands.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you spot that detecting 'fully surrounded' directly is awkward, and invert it to 'reachable from the border'. Also whether you mark safe cells with a temporary state and restore them cleanly.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Trying to detect enclosure with a flood fill that 'returns false if it hits the edge' — correct but fiddly and easy to get wrong. Or forgetting to restore the '#' markers back to 'O'.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Lead with the inversion ('mark what escapes, flip what's left'), give both DFS and BFS (BFS avoids stack overflow on huge boards), and mention the Union-Find-with-a-virtual-border-node formulation.

problemStatement:
Given an `m x n` matrix `board` containing `'X'` and `'O'`, **capture all regions that are 4-directionally surrounded by `'X'`**.

A region is captured by flipping all `'O'`s into `'X'`s in that surrounded region.

Notice that an `'O'` should **not** be flipped if it is on the border, or if it is connected (4-directionally) to an `'O'` that is on the border.

Modify `board` in place; you do not return anything.
understanding: An 'O' is 'safe' if and only if it can reach the grid border through other 'O's. Every other 'O' is part of a region entirely walled in by 'X' and must be captured. We don't count regions — we flip the trapped ones to 'X' in place.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are diagonal cells considered connected?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — only the 4 orthogonal neighbours (up/down/left/right). I'd confirm, since 8-directional would change which regions count as enclosed.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I modify the board in place, and what do I return?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The signature returns void and expects in-place mutation. I'll use a temporary marker on safe cells and clean it up before finishing.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How big can the board get?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to 200×200 = 40,000 cells. A recursive DFS could approach that depth on a board that's almost all 'O', so I'd consider iterative BFS to avoid a stack overflow.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is a single-row or single-column board possible?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. In a 1×n or m×1 board every cell is on the border, so nothing is ever captured — my border seeding handles that automatically.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Border flood fill (DFS/BFS) is the default; Union-Find for a connectivity-flavored framing.

approaches.name: Border DFS — Mark Escapees, Flip the Rest
approaches.whenToMention: Lead with this. Phrase it as 'I won't look for surrounded regions; I'll look for the ones that escape to the border, then flip whatever is left'.
hints: Detecting 'this region is fully surrounded' from the inside is awkward — you'd have to track whether the fill ever touched an edge. Can you flip the question to make it easy?
An 'O' is safe exactly when it can reach the border. So flood-fill starting from every 'O' on the four edges and mark everything reachable as 'safe'.
After marking, sweep the whole board: any 'O' left was never reached from the border → it's enclosed, flip it to 'X'. Then turn your 'safe' markers back into 'O'.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each cell is visited a constant number of times: once by border seeding / a flood fill, and once by the final flip sweep → O(m × n). Recursion can descend to the size of one connected 'O' region, up to O(m × n) on an almost-all-'O' board.
approaches.explanation:
The breakthrough is refusing to solve the literal question. Asking 'is this region surrounded?' forces you to explore a region and somehow remember whether it ever brushed the boundary — a flood fill that must thread a boolean back up through recursion. It works, but it's error-prone.

**Invert it.** A region is captured *unless* it can escape to the edge. The complement — 'can this 'O' reach the border?' — is trivial to compute: start from the border and flood inward. So we seed a DFS from every `'O'` sitting in row 0, the last row, column 0, or the last column. Anything those fills reach is, by definition, connected to the outside and therefore **safe**. We stamp each safe cell with a temporary marker `'#'`.

**Why the temporary marker matters.** After the border fills finish, the board holds three kinds of cells: `'X'` (walls), `'#'` (safe `'O'`s that escaped), and `'O'` (the ones the fills never reached). That last group is exactly the enclosed regions. The final sweep makes two replacements: every surviving `'O'` becomes `'X'` (captured), and every `'#'` is restored to `'O'` (it was always safe). Skipping the restore step leaves the board littered with `'#'` — a wrong answer that's easy to overlook in testing.

**Why DFS is enough.** We're not measuring distances or sizes; we only need to *reach* every escapee. DFS does that with a four-way recursion and a single base case: stop when out of bounds or when the cell isn't an `'O'`. The marker `'#'` doubles as the visited flag, so cells are never re-entered and the recursion terminates.

**Why I'd flag the recursion depth.** On a 200×200 board that's almost all `'O'`, the fill can recurse ~40,000 frames deep and overflow the call stack in languages with modest limits. That's the cue to offer the iterative BFS version, which moves the frontier into a heap-allocated queue.
approaches.insight: The captured regions are the *complement* of the border-reachable region. Whenever a grid asks you to find cells that are 'trapped inside', the cheap move is almost always to flood-fill from the outside and keep what you didn't touch.

approaches.name: Border BFS — Iterative Frontier
approaches.whenToMention: Offer when the board is large enough to risk recursion-stack overflow. Same O(m × n), explicit queue instead of the call stack.
hints: Same inversion as DFS — mark border-reachable 'O's safe — but expand the frontier with an explicit queue instead of recursion.
First enqueue (and mark) every 'O' on the four borders. Then repeatedly dequeue a cell and enqueue its unmarked 'O' neighbours.
Mark cells at ENQUEUE time, not dequeue time, so the same cell is never queued twice.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each cell enters and leaves the queue at most once → O(m × n). The final flip sweep is another O(m × n). The queue can hold up to a large frontier, O(m × n) in the worst case.
approaches.explanation:
The logic is byte-for-byte the same as the DFS version — find what escapes to the border, capture the rest — but the traversal is iterative, which is what makes it safe at scale.

**Why iterative matters here.** A recursive border fill on a 200×200 board that is almost entirely `'O'` can stack ~40,000 frames and overflow the call stack in stack-limited environments. BFS relocates that frontier into a heap-allocated queue, so the depth of exploration never touches the call stack.

**Seed first, then expand.** We make one initial pass over the four borders, and for each `'O'` we find we mark it `'#'` and enqueue it. That primes the queue with every entry point to the outside. Then the main loop pops a cell, inspects its four orthogonal neighbours, and for each in-bounds `'O'` it marks `'#'` and enqueues — extending the safe region outward layer by layer.

**Mark on enqueue, never on dequeue.** This is the one BFS detail that bites people. If you wait until a cell is dequeued to mark it, multiple neighbours can enqueue the same cell before it's processed, inflating the queue and re-doing work. Marking the instant you enqueue guarantees each cell is added exactly once.

**Same final sweep.** Once the queue drains, the board again has `'X'` walls, `'#'` escapees, and trapped `'O'`s. The closing double-flip — `'O' → 'X'`, `'#' → 'O'` — finishes the job identically to the DFS approach.
approaches.insight: DFS and BFS are interchangeable for *reachability* — both just need to touch every border-connected 'O'. BFS is the safer default at scale because its memory lives in an explicit queue, not in recursion depth that can blow the stack.

approaches.name: Union-Find with a Virtual Border Node
approaches.whenToMention: Mention as the connectivity-flavored alternative, especially if the interviewer steers toward Union-Find. Same asymptotic cost with near-constant α.
hints: Model each cell as a node. Add one extra 'virtual' node that represents 'the outside / the border'.
Union every border 'O' with the virtual node, and union each 'O' with its 'O' neighbours below and to the right.
After all unions, an 'O' is safe iff it shares a root with the virtual node. Every other 'O' is captured.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each cell does a constant number of unions/finds; with path compression and union the amortized cost per operation is α (inverse Ackermann), effectively constant → O(m × n × α).
approaches.explanation:
Union-Find reframes 'reachable from the border' as 'in the same set as a single virtual node that stands for the outside'.

**The virtual node trick.** Create one sentinel id (say `rows * cols`) that means 'connected to the border'. As we scan the grid, every `'O'` that lies on an edge gets unioned with this sentinel. That collapses the question 'can this cell escape?' into 'does this cell's set contain the sentinel?' — a single `find` comparison at the end.

**Building the rest of the connectivity.** For each `'O'`, we union it with its `'O'` neighbour directly below and directly to the right. Checking only down and right (rather than all four directions) is enough because every orthogonal adjacency is covered exactly once as we sweep the grid in row-major order — the up/left edges are handled when the *other* endpoint is processed. This halves the union calls without missing any connection.

**The final classification.** After the unions, we sweep once more. An `'O'` is captured precisely when `find(cell) != find(virtual)` — i.e. it never joined the outside's set. Those flip to `'X'`; everything else stays. Because we never used a temporary marker, there's no restore step.

**Why path compression and the α bound.** The `find` here flattens the tree as it walks (pointing each node at its grandparent), so repeated queries get cheaper. Combined over `m × n` cells, the total work is `O(m × n × α(m × n))`, where α is the inverse Ackermann function — at most 4 for any board you could ever allocate, so effectively linear. The flood-fill solutions are simpler to write under interview pressure; reach for Union-Find when the conversation is explicitly about disjoint-set structures or dynamic connectivity.
approaches.insight: A single virtual node that represents 'the boundary' turns a reachability question into a set-membership question. That sentinel pattern recurs whenever 'connected to a special place' is the property you care about.

Forgetting to restore the temporary '#' markers back to 'O' in the final sweep.
Seeding the flood fill from only some of the four borders.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting to restore the safe markers
commonMistakesDetailed.why: After the border fill, safe cells carry the temporary '#'. The final sweep must turn '#' back into 'O'; otherwise the output board is littered with stray markers and fails the judge.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Solving the problem directly instead of inverting
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Detecting enclosure from the inside means a flood fill that must report whether it ever touched an edge and only flip if it didn't — extra state, easy to get wrong. Marking border-reachable cells safe is simpler and robust.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Marking BFS cells on dequeue instead of enqueue
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you only mark a cell when you pop it, several neighbours can enqueue the same cell first, so it is processed multiple times and the queue balloons.

followupVariations.title: Number of Islands
followupVariations.hint: The foundational grid flood fill — count connected components of land instead of inverting from the border.

followupVariations.title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
followupVariations.hint: Same border-seeding idea, run twice (from each ocean), then intersect the reachable sets.

followupVariations.title: Number of Closed Islands
followupVariations.hint: Flood-fill border-touching land first to disqualify it, then count the remaining fully-enclosed islands.

followupVariations.title: Max Area of Island
followupVariations.hint: Same flood fill, but return the size of each region and track the maximum.

patternNote: Inversion + border flood fill. When 'trapped inside' is hard to test, flood-fill from the outside and keep what you didn't reach. Same family as Number of Islands, Pacific Atlantic Water Flow, and Number of Closed Islands; Union-Find with a virtual node is the connectivity-flavored alternative.
